questions.q: Which is a missing row, not a missing value?
options: There is no entry for 3 January at all
The entry for 3 January has NaN
why: Correct. The timestamp is absent from the index.
That is a missing value: the row exists.
That is a hidden missing value.

questions.q: A series is 10, NaN, NaN, 22. Linear interpolation: what is the value at the third position?
questions.why: The step is (22 − 10) / 3 = 4 per position. The values are 10, 14, 18, 22.

questions.q: s = [5, NaN, NaN, 9]. What does s.ffill(limit=1) give for the last NaN?
why: Correct. limit=1 fills only the first missing step after a value. The second NaN stays.
ffill fills the first NaN with 5, but with limit=1 not the second.
ffill never uses a later value.

questions.q: Why is s.fillna(s.mean()) on the whole series risky before a time split?
options: The mean contains the test period (future information)
why: Correct. Compute fill statistics on the training period only.
The mean can be fine as a value. The problem is where it is computed.

questions.q: A shop's daily sales table has no row for Sundays, because the shop is closed. For a daily model, what should Sundays be?
why: Correct. Closed means true zero. Add the rows so the weekly pattern stays visible.
Interpolation invents sales that did not happen.
Dropping rows breaks the weekly rhythm and the lags.

questions.q: A model predicts hour t+1 using a feature built from the hourly sensor value. You must fill gaps in the feature. Which is leak-free?
options: ffill, then add a was_missing flag
why: Correct. Only past values are used, and the flag shows which values were filled.

questions.q: You want to attach to each trade the latest known interest rate published before it. Which pandas tool?
why: Correct. merge_asof matches on the nearest earlier time.
concat stacks tables. It does not match by time.
interpolate fills NaN inside one table.
